title: how to start?
author: Shppo
selftext:
ever since i was a kid, i’ve wanted to make my own video game. i’ve experimented with things like level editors and rpg maker from time to time, but unfortunately, i never really learned how to code.

for the past few months, i’ve been seeing incredibly impressive games in this community, some of them apparently made by people who don’t have any coding skills either. i’d love to start developing a game with ai, but i’m a little overwhelmed by all the possibilities. new tools are constantly being released in the ai space.

fortunately, i’m not a complete beginner when it comes to ai. i’ve already worked quite a bit with generative ai in particular, but i’ve never tried developing a game before. given the current state of things, which tools, models, or workflows would you recommend?

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body:
I feel like you should get some subscription that you prefer (I use Claude) then see what it can do with simple promts. Even like:

Hey I want to build xyz how do we start.

Then once you start getting into it you pick engine (currently Godot is most popular but Unity works also or just make directly in Browser as most people do).

Then you start getting more into it you will knoe toold for 3D and MCP for blender or Godot and so on. I think by the time you even decide what you want to build you will learn so much more. 

Don’t be afraid to fail and start from 0 because you most certainly will. From all the games you see here probably 1% finds it’s way to the market… if so.

replies.body: Unreal is a bad choice because afaik lots of the game files aren't stored in plain text. Unity and Godot both have basically everything in plain text, so they are super easy for LLMs to read and change.

replies.author: Tok-A-Mak
replies.body:
Depends on the type of game you wanna make. 

For generative games that don't require a manually created map, Godot > Other Engines because it can be used 100% headless without ever touching the editor and without using any MCPs or any of that stuff. It's just so much simpler if you can work around all of that.

My suggestion: Claude Code or similar (not Claude Desktop). You run it in a Linux shell or in WSL or maybe in Docker if you're on Windows. Then you ask it to download Godot Mono and Blender binaries for it's own use. You also ask it to install Python so it can properly script Blender. You ask it for some basic shell scripts, such as start.sh, run-tests.sh, print-stats.sh, build-releases.sh, whatever you need.

Then you tell it what game to make, probably in like a specs(.)md and that's pretty much it.

Use Git right away and ask it to "keep the core pure" and to create tests for everything that's pure. For animations, ARDY scripted with Python, although very basic locomotion is something Claude may do directly rather.

Use cheap and efficient models to create the whole setup and consider switching to expensive models only on special occasions, such as for creating the initial scaffold of the game core or when creating complex new systems.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: UE is a great engine. But it's not that great for vibecoding. If you're willing to spend hundreds of hours learning the engine yourself, then AI can be a good assistant even within UE. But if that sounds too daunting for you then you need to dial back to an engine AI can do the heavy lifting in.

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body:
I use Godot for my engine and codex works perfectly with it.  I recommend trying to build in Godot without codex first though, so that you get familiar with the node types.  I started 8 months ago, but just hooked codex up last week.  while im very glad I did it, and its certainly impressive, im glad I spent the time without it so I have a better idea of what it's doing.   chatgpt helped walk through Godot and explain the engine UI and answered all my initial questions.

aseprite is also good if you are looking into pixel art, as you can import generated images and edit and scale as needed.

replies.author: Ahenian
replies.body: Codex is usable on free tier as well.

comments.author: That1guy4226
comments.body: I highly recommend starting with either Claude or Codex. A 20 dollar sub is plenty to get you started. Take the time to ask it to help get you setup properly. You absolutely can make games with the popular game engines if you make sure that your agent has proper access and a clear understanding of your vision. Even without a tech or dev background.

comments.author: CordusPorf
comments.body: I've been using opencode with Deepseek V4 Pro(it's very cheap and very good, $25 bucks can last a month of heavy usage), blender-mcp and unity-mcp for creating assets in blender and geting them into Unity. comments.author: Additional_Thanks927
comments.body:
I think research is basically always how to start.some things are preference like do u wanna develop in the cloud or do u wanna develop on u're local machine ...then u need to asses your skills what are u're strengths and weaknesses and how do the models compliment my skill set...then u need to budget. Ask yourself what is my maximum spend that I'm willing to literally light on fire in case this fails something like 96 percent of indie game devs fail to ever turn a profit....then u need to do market research and come up with a great plan and understand what makes games in that genre great....then create a scope,mvp,milestone,design plan,asset pipeline and marketing/publishing text documents/md files.... Review your plans then EXECUTE preforming manual and automated testing after every defined deliverable...plz remember that u will need some token spend to fix everything ai delivers/balance the game and ull probably need some tokens to modify the game after u get feedback about what people like dislike

tldr summary: make the docs listed below using ai to help u and you'll basically know everything u need to deliver and test 

create a scope,minimym viable product,milestone,design plan/rules,asset pipeline and marketing/publishing plan as text documents/md files


Optional advice: once u begin development u're locked into plan tell post publish and feedback I've seen so many projects die to scope creep/budget/token limits also might not be the worst idea to define optional cuttable features organized by complexity in u're docs.in case u get 3 quarters of the way there and it starts to look like u're out of runway to early. Put simply its easy to find something else to develop but even if u made 99.999 percent of a mvp it ain't gonna do u or anyone else much good

comments.author: ChirpXel
comments.body:
Pick a engine. 
Pick an AI
Download an MCP so they AI can interact with the engine. 
Ask the AI to teach you how to use the engine, and basics of building a game. 
DONT ask it to fully create the game for you
Spend time learning the tools and engine yourself.
Then have the AI help in building the pieces of the game with you once you have a better understanding of what your doing.

comments.author: IllustriousCulture22
comments.body: io qualche anno fa ero nella tua stessa situazione, cominciai con Claude ma all'epoca non era molto potente, passai a Replit e da allora mi sono sempre affidato a lui. Claude potrebbe essere oggi più performante? Forse sì, il problema è proprio che stiamo vivendo in una transizione in cui ogni mese emergono AI sempre più potenti. Lo scoglio principale rimane sempre il game design, l'AI non è in grado di farlo in maniera efficace, e mi rendo conto che lavorare da soli è sempre un limite.
